searchText: Have merged this 🙂 One thing I think we need to explain is why each suffix node is committed to using two pedersen commitments C1 and C2 as you noted and not just 1 pedersen commitment. I wasn’t sure if that document was the right place to put it, or if there will be a separate document focussed solely on the different types of nodes Writing reason here incase it’s not available anywhere else: each value is 32 bytes/256 bits, but the structure which will hold the values (field elements) can only store ~253 bits of information, it essentially truncates the top 3 bits away. So we instead split the 32-byte value into its low and high 128 bit components. Since we can only commit to 256 things with pedersen, and each suffix node holds 256 32-byte values, when we split it up, we will have 512 values, so we need two commitments to commit to all of the values. https://blog.ethereum.org/2021/12/02/verkle-tree-structure This article was great for me to understand the underlying go-verkle implemention. It explains that with detail. Ah forgot about that, thanks for the relink Sweet. Ahh gotcha yea will include that in a future PR. Is this limit of being able to commit to only 256 things an implementation detail from the spec, rather than an intrinsic mathematical property of the Pedersen commitment? Yep it’s an implementation detail, in the past, the node width used to be 1024 instead of 256 1024 allowed for shallower tries due to more children being on a single level, but it was not nice to use since 10 bits crosses over two byte boundaries whereas 8 bits fits perfectly inside of a byte

Have merged this 🙂 One thing I think we need to explain is why each suffix node is committed to using two pedersen commitments C1 and C2 as you noted and not just 1 pedersen commitment.

I wasn’t sure if that document was the right place to put it, or if there will be a separate document focussed solely on the different types of nodes

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content:
Writing reason here incase it’s not available anywhere else: each value is 32 bytes/256 bits, but the structure which will hold the values (field elements) can only store ~253 bits of information, it essentially truncates the top 3 bits away. So we instead split the 32-byte value into its low and high 128 bit components. 

Since we can only commit to 256 things with pedersen, and each suffix node holds 256 32-byte values, when we split it up, we will have 512 values, so we need two commitments to commit to all of the values.

Is this limit of being able to commit to only 256 things an implementation detail from the spec, rather than an intrinsic mathematical property of the Pedersen commitment?

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content: Yep it’s an implementation detail, in the past, the node width used to be 1024 instead of 256

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content: 1024 allowed for shallower tries due to more children being on a single level, but it was not nice to use since 10 bits crosses over two byte boundaries whereas 8 bits fits perfectly inside of a byte
